newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: COMPENSATION CHANGES LIKELY FOR POWER SURGES
New legal advice to the Australian Compeition and Consumer Commission could mean power companies are liable to pay ompensation for damage caused by power surges.
At present, power companies don't accept any blame if equipment is ruined or fires break-out as a result of a surge.

But A-triple-C chairman, Alan Fels, says under a new reading of the Trade Practices Act, power companies are liable for damage in the event of surges or reduced supply, whether it's their fault or not.
Professor Fels says if a surge causes great damage to a consumers appliance, it would seem that the electricity is not fit for the purpose intended.
UNION VOWS TO FIGHT SHIPPING OVERHAUL
The Maritime Union says the Federal Government will set the scene for industrial conflict if it accepts recommendations of a report to be released today.
The Manser Report's expected to recommend an overhaul of ship employment practices, allowing foreign ships on domestic coastal routes, and setting up a second register of Australian ships.
The union's John Coombes says the Union's steadfastly opposed to the proposals, but the Australian Shipowners Association says the changes are vital for the future health of shipping.
Mr Coombes says unless there's consultation, the Government's heading for a massive dispute.
COURT WARNS OF DANGERS OF RACIST TAG
West Australian Premier Richard Court has warned of the dangers of being labelled a racist for speaking out.
Mr Court's comments came during debate on a successful motion to denounce racial tolerance, and support federal parliament's committment to maintaining a non-discriminatory immigration policy.
Mr Court says he was once called a racist for speaking out.
But he says people should place themsleves in the shoes of an Aboriginal person to understand the hurt of the current racist debate.

Aboriginal MP, Ernie Bridge, says racial harmony in Australia has deteriorated. Mr Bridge says he doubts the 1960's referendum to grant Aborigines full citizenship would recieve as much support if it were held again in 1997.
POLICE INVESTIGATING DOUBLE MURDER
Police are interviewing a 26-year-old man about the murder of two women overnight in the Wollongong suburb of Dapto.
The police went to a house and found the body of a 24-year-old woman in a hallway, and a 54-year-old woman in a bedroom.
The police were responding to a call from the man they're now interviewing, who was at the house when they arrived.
The two women were the man's sister and mother.
The police say they apparently were strangled following a domestic dispute.
40 CHILD SEX CHARGES DROPPED IN BELL CASE
Alleged paedophile Phillip Bell has lost his appeal against Australia's attempts to extradite him from South Africa to face child sex charges.
62 year-old Bell has now instructed his lawyers to seek leave to appeal the ruling in South Africa's highest court.
If that fails he has 21 days to petition the South African Chief Justice.
The court also ordered that 40 of the charges be dropped because they allegedly occured before 1977 and have expired under South Africa's statute of limitations.
Bell's lawyer Neil Paterson says the ruling means his client will only face the remaining 175 charges if and when he returns to Australia.
Once all legal avenues have been exhausted it's expected to take less than a week to complete Bell's extradition.
HANSON MORE OF A WORRY THAN JOH FOR PM, SAYS BORBIDGE
Queensland's Premier, Rob Borbidge, says the difference between Pauline Hanson and the Joh for PM campaign is that this time people are having their property taken from them.
Mr Borbidge says the Prime Minister is missing the point if he doesn't recognise the danger of Pauline Hanson to the conservative parties.
He says he's in touch with the views of rural Australia, and there's growing anger about John Howard's refusal to extinguish Native Title on pastoral leases.
PM HAS DAMAGED CONVENTION'S CREDIBILITY - BOLKUS
Federal Labor front-bencher, Nick Bolkus, says the Prime Minister can't be trusted to organise the delegates list for this year's Constitutional Convention.
Mr Bolkus says the Government's failure to publically advertise for delegates further damages the credibility of the Convention.
The deadline for public nominations for Convention places closes tomorrow and the Government says it has simply written to interest groups asking for their nominees.
Of the seventy-six appointed Convention delegates, thirty-six will be members of the public and the Government insists this group will be broadly representative.
